title: Deterministic Verification and a Single-Repair Guardrail for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: a Paired, Shared‑Candidate Study
abstract: We report a sealed, preregistered paired experiment that measured the verifier-confirmed marginal effect of inserting a deterministic validator plus up to one automated repair (a guarded generate–verify–repair pipeline) on the same LLM-generated configuration candidate. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics we produced one initial candidate per natural-language intent with gpt-5-mini for N = 250 intent pairs and evaluated two episodes per intent: baseline (accept candidate as-is) and guarded (deterministic_netops_validator_v5; if it failed, permit one automated repair). Execution completed 500 episodes with model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial generations + 1 repair). Results: baseline verifier-pass 249/250 (99.6%), guarded verifier-pass 250/250 (100.0%); paired contingency n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = +0.4 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp] (paired bootstrap percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The single discordant pair was converted to pass by the single permitted repair. We explicitly disclose a preregistration–execution deviation (the preregistration framed a sim‑to‑real emulation vs production-like confirmatory comparison that was not executed); the executed confirmatory estimand is the paired guarded−baseline difference on the synthetic/emulation partition. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived and referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being explored as intent-to-configuration translators in network operations (NetOps), promising faster authoring of device CLI sequences and intent-driven automation. However, stochastic generation creates operational risk: syntax errors, incorrect command ordering, local-policy violations, and vendor-CLI subtleties can produce unsafe or non-functional device changes. Prior studies demonstrate that LLMs can produce usable draft configurations but typically require verification or human oversight to reach acceptable operational assurance [1,2].

A common architectural response is an interposed deterministic validator and, where appropriate, automated repair templates — a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline — that accepts only validator-passed candidates or attempts bounded repair when the verifier detects mechanically testable defects [3–5]. While GVR architectures reduce mechanically verifiable error classes, open questions remain about their marginal benefit when modern LLM outputs are already highly consistent with validator encodings and about pipeline accounting under paired experimental semantics.

This paper reports a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment that isolates the marginal effect of inserting a deterministic validator plus a single automated repair on the same initial LLM candidate. The confirmatory estimand (as executed) compares verifier-confirmed intent-satisfaction when the same generated candidate is accepted versus when the deterministic validator and up to one automated repair are applied. The study focuses on a constrained synthetic/emulation partition and is designed under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure only the validator+repair marginal effect on identical model outputs.
sections.related_work:
Recent community surveys and experimental studies have described intent-driven configuration generation and the associated verification needs for NetOps [1,2]. Evaluations such as NetConfEval show feasibility of LLMs for configuration tasks under emulation but highlight persistent syntactic and local-policy errors that motivate verification layers [1]. Critical analyses of LLM self-correction indicate that reliable self-fixation typically depends on dependable external signals or verifiers rather than unconstrained in‑model correction [2].

Work on deterministic verification, formal analysis, and tooling (e.g., Batfish-style analyses, header-space and model-checking techniques) provides validated mechanisms for checking reachability and policy properties and has been applied as validator components in GVR-like pipelines [4,3]. Research in code/configuration generate-and-verify repair shows that applying deterministic checks plus template-driven repairs can remove mechanically verifiable defects, though semantic correctness and cross-vendor behavior remain hard to ensure [5]. Threat analyses of prompt-injection and LLM-integrated application attacks underscore the value of filter/validator layers but also show that adaptive adversaries are an unresolved threat [6]. Our study situates itself at the intersection of these lines by measuring the marginal verifier+single-repair effect on identical LLM outputs under a preregistered, paired design.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered as study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1. The preregistration specified a paired design with N_pairs = 250, generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, and the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The confirmatory contract for this run applied to the synthetic/emulation partition only; the preregistered sim-to-real contrast (emulation vs production-like) was not executed and is explicitly disclosed.

Under shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one initial generation call was produced per intent and that same generated candidate was reused for both episodes (baseline and guarded). This design therefore isolates only the marginal effect of validation and permitted repair on the identical candidate rather than conflating prompt/prompting or sampling variability across conditions. The execution manifest and deterministic reconciliation artifacts in the archive document provider-call accounting (see archived deterministic_reconciliation.json and provider_call_audit summary for reconciled call counts and stage breakdown).

Task generation, model, and guarded pipeline. A deterministic task generator produced 250 constrained intent tasks (intent templates and expected sequences). Each intent produced one shared initial candidate from the declared model gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). Episodes per intent: baseline — accept the shared initial candidate as-is and submit to the deterministic validator; guarded — evaluate the same shared candidate with deterministic_netops_validator_v5; if the validator failed, permit up to one automated repair call following the preregistered repair template. Repairs used preregistered, template-driven transformation attempts only; no iterative repair beyond one attempt was allowed.

Provider-call accounting and reconciliation semantics. The archive records model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial_generation calls + 1 repair). The deterministic_reconciliation artifact (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json, archive manifest) contains provider_call_audit showing hosted_model_call_event_count = 251 and stage_counts {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1}. Condition_counts in the audit reflect instrumentation labeling (e.g., {"shared": 250, "guarded": 1}) rather than implying separate first-pass generations per condition; this labeling arises from how adapter-stage instrumentation records pipeline stages under the shared_initial_candidate contract. In other words, stage_counts enumerate actual model-call stages (generation, repair) while condition_counts reflect recorded stage-labeling and should not be misread as independent per-condition first-pass generations. The deterministic_reconciliation artifact reconciles these fields and the episode accounting (planned_episode_count = 500, completed_episode_count = 500) and confirms that all completed episodes derive from 250 shared initial candidates plus the single permitted repair call.
sections.results:
Execution and primary outcomes. Execution completed as a confirmatory run: planned_episode_count = 500, completed_episode_count = 500, complete_pair_count = 250, model_calls_used = 251. The deterministic validator produced binary verifier_pass outcomes under the preregistered full_intent_constraint_validation rules.

Primary aggregated counts (archive artifacts analysis/condition_summary.csv and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): baseline_success_count = 249 (baseline_success_rate = 0.996), guarded_success_count = 250 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Contingency table (guarded × baseline): n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.004 (0.4 percentage points). Exact McNemar two‑sided test as preregistered produced p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval on the paired difference (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.012] (0 – 1.2 percentage points). The single discordant pair (n10 = 1) was converted to pass by the single permitted repair (repair-conversion = 1/250 = 0.4%). No preregistered exclusions or contamination flags occurred for the confirmatory partition; missingness_summary reports 250 complete pairs.

Representative artifacts and diagnostics. Representative task, shared-initial response, validator trace, and scoring records are archived for sampled tasks (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json). Validator traces include parsed_command_count, required_command_count, final_state snapshots, and explicit violation codes when present; in the confirmatory partition all validation_after entries reported valid = true for passed episodes. Analysis artifacts with contingency and condition summaries are available (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; analysis/condition_summary.csv). The archived analysis log records bootstrap parameters (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729) and the paired-analysis completion event.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and practical bounds. The executed confirmatory comparison, limited to the synthetic/emulation partition and under shared_initial_candidate semantics, indicates a near-null marginal effect of inserting a deterministic validator plus a single automated repair on modern LLM-generated candidates in this constrained task regime: initial LLM candidates already satisfied the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases. The observed baseline pass (0.996) substantially exceeded the preregistration assumption (≈0.90), reducing power for detecting small positive guarded effects. The paired bootstrap CI upper bound (1.2 percentage points) provides an empirical bound on the possible verifier-improvement under the studied configuration and pipeline.

Why the marginal effect was small here. Several artifact-grounded factors explain the small guarded gain: (1) the task generator constrained intents and limited allowed touched fields, reducing the space of acceptable variations; (2) the model and prompt templates produced well-formed, validator-consistent candidate sequences in most sampled intents; (3) the deterministic validator checked mechanically verifiable workflow and syntactic properties but not richer runtime semantics. These points are documented in task payloads and validator traces in the archive (task_manifest entries include allowed_fields, required_sequence, and difficulty patterns).

Threats to validity and scope. Internal validity: results depend on the precise prompt templates, the declared model (gpt-5-mini), the single-repair policy, and the shared_initial_candidate design. Construct validity: the deterministic validator assessed mechanically verifiable properties (syntax, workflow ordering) and does not assert behavioral correctness in live protocol operation or performance. External validity: the confirmatory evidence covers the synthetic/emulation partition only; the preregistered community and production-like partitions were not executed and remain for future evaluation. Security: adaptive prompt-injection and retrieval-based adversaries were not exercised. Conclusion: while GVR guardrails are conceptually valuable, in tightly constrained emulation-style tasks with a capable LLM their marginal verifier-detected benefit may be limited; this does not imply they are unnecessary in broader or adversarial operational contexts.
sections.conclusion: We executed a sealed, preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure the verifier-detected marginal benefit of deterministic validation plus a single automated repair on identical LLM-generated configuration candidates. In N = 250 constrained synthetic intent tasks, initial gpt-5-mini candidates passed the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases; the guarded pipeline converted the single failing candidate. Paired improvement = 0.4 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp]; p = 1.0). We explicitly disclose that the preregistered sim‑to‑real confirmatory comparison was not executed and that the executed confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline evaluated on the synthetic/emulation partition only. Broader production, adversarial, and partition‑specific evaluations remain necessary to establish external generality. All execution manifests, raw responses, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis artifacts referenced in this paper are archived and available in the evidence bundle described in the Disclosure Statement.

disclosure_statement:
Human role and autonomy boundary: After an autonomy lock required by the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track, the autonomous system performed literature search, study selection, preregistration freeze, prompt preservation, model calls, deterministic validation, permitted repair execution, analysis, drafting, peer-review, revision, and finalization without manual human editing of technical content. A human Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and performed pre-lock infrastructure development only; no human manually edited manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.

Models, tools, and framework: declared model = gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; deterministic task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Execution used a guarded generate–verify–repair flow permitting at most one automated repair per episode as specified in the preregistration.

Preregistration and immutable prompt references (archived): preregistration study id = study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1; preregistration artifact SHA-256 = 7a984dbf7265c9a774eaf95c6c930dcf5f1e8845088bbc0e0855e3b4f1000ede. Immutable master prompt used to initiate the autonomous run: provenance/master_prompt.txt, SHA-256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Execution manifest and analysis artifacts (manifests, raw responses, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis outputs) are archived in the evidence bundle; the archive contains deterministic_reconciliation and analysis artifacts that document provider-call accounting and stage_counts.

Executed confirmatory estimand and deviation disclosure: The preregistration included multiple partitions (synthetic/emulation, community, production-like) and a preregistered sim-to-real confirmatory contrast. Deviation disclosure (explicit): the preregistered sim-to-real confirmatory comparison was not executed in this run; the executed confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline evaluated on the synthetic/emulation partition only (N_pairs = 250; shared_initial_candidate semantics). Provider-call accounting in the archive reconciles to model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial_generation + 1 repair) and stage_counts {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1}, consistent with the shared_initial_candidate design. Full execution and analysis manifests and per-artifact hashes are archived and referenced in the evidence bundle.
limitations: Confirmatory scope limited to the synthetic/emulation partition; preregistered community and production-like partitions were not executed and remain exploratory.

Deterministic validator assessed mechanically verifiable properties (syntax and prescribed workflow sequences) but did not measure broader semantic or behavioral correctness (protocol dynamics, emergent interactions).
Single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator implementation were used; results do not establish multi-model or alternate-validator generality.
Only one automated repair attempt was permitted by design; multi-iteration repairs or human-in-the-loop escalation were not evaluated.
Adversarial and retrieval-based attacks (adaptive prompt-injection, vendor-targeted exploit vectors) and large-scale production heterogeneity were not exercised and remain open threats.
